title: Secondhand: What Gets Lost When We Report What Others Say
paragraphs: There is a well-known communication game — sometimes called Chinese Whispers, or Telephone — in which a message is whispered from person to person along a chain. By the time it reaches the end, it has almost always been transformed, sometimes beyond recognition. The game is usually played for amusement, but it illustrates something important and a little unsettling: that human communication is extraordinarily good at producing meaning, and extraordinarily bad at preserving it accurately.

This principle extends far beyond childhood games. In professional, academic, and journalistic contexts, the process of reporting what someone said — converting their words into reported speech — inevitably involves interpretation. The reporter must decide which words to reproduce, which to paraphrase, which to omit. They must decide which reporting verb to use, which pieces of context to include, and how much of the original tone to preserve. Every one of these decisions introduces a small degree of interpretive distance between the original speaker and the eventual audience.

Researchers who study how information travels through social networks have documented a consistent pattern: each "relay" in a chain of communication tends to reduce the total amount of information transmitted while increasing the proportion that reflects the relayer's own perspective. By the time a message has been reported three or four times — journalist reports a speech, newspaper article is summarised by a blog, blog post is shared on social media with a comment — the original meaning may be almost unrecognisable.

The problem is compounded by the natural tendency of human memory to reconstruct rather than replay. When Rustam reports to Kamila what his professor said in last week's seminar, he is not playing back a recording. He is reconstructing the experience from memory — and memory, psychologists have established beyond reasonable doubt, is not a passive recorder but an active interpreter. Rustam remembers what seemed important to him, what resonated with things he already believed, and what confirmed or challenged his existing views. His report of what the professor said will inevitably carry Rustam's own perspective even when he is trying to be as accurate as possible.

This does not mean that reported speech is unreliable or that we should distrust all secondhand accounts. It means that all reported speech must be understood as a version — shaped by the choices of the reporter, the limitations of memory, and the constraints of the medium. The question to ask of any reported account is not "Is this true?" but rather "Whose version is this, and what might they have emphasised, omitted, or reinterpreted?"

In academic writing, this is why proper citation matters so much. When you write "Smith argued that..." you are representing the work of another scholar, and your reader trusts that you have done this responsibly. Choosing the wrong reporting verb, summarising inaccurately, or omitting crucial context are all forms of misrepresentation — even if they are entirely unintentional.

For students working at B1 and above, the practical implication is this: reported speech is not merely a grammatical exercise. It is an act of representation that carries responsibility. Whether you are summarising a lecture, reporting a conversation, writing a news article, or citing a source in an essay, you are making choices about how someone else's words will be received. Those choices matter — grammatically, ethically, and epistemically.

dialogue.speaker: Daniyar
dialogue.text: I told Amir what you said in your presentation yesterday. He seemed interested.

dialogue.speaker: Kamila
dialogue.text: What did you tell him exactly?

dialogue.speaker: Daniyar
dialogue.text: That you argued that journalism shapes public opinion more than politicians do.

dialogue.speaker: Kamila
dialogue.text: I said journalism can sometimes be as powerful as policy. That's quite different.

dialogue.speaker: Daniyar
dialogue.text: I thought that was what you meant.

dialogue.speaker: Kamila
dialogue.text: Exactly — that's the problem. You reported what you thought I meant, not what I said.

dialogue.speaker: Daniyar
dialogue.text: So your version is more cautious. Mine sounds like a much stronger claim.

dialogue.speaker: Kamila
dialogue.text: And once it's out there, it's my name attached to Amir's version of your version of my words.

keyPhrases.context: "Secondhand accounts." = information received through another person, not directly.
"Reporting inevitably involves interpretation." = it always happens, cannot be avoided.
"Interpretive distance between speaker and audience." = the gap created by reporting.
"The problem is compounded by..." = made worse by an additional factor.
"Memory reconstructs rather than replays." = builds back up, not plays back.
"Each relay in a chain." = each time information is passed from one person to another.
"Forms of misrepresentation." = presenting something falsely or inaccurately.
"Matters epistemically." = from the perspective of how we know and understand things.

vocab.definition: to build or create again; to put together from parts or memory
vocab.example: Memory reconstructs rather than replays — it is an active process, not a recording.

vocab.definition: as is certain to happen; unavoidably
vocab.example: Reporting what someone said inevitably involves some degree of interpretation.

vocab.definition: passing something (message) from one person/place to another
vocab.example: Each relay in the chain reduces information and adds the relayer's perspective.

vocab.definition: to make worse by adding to; to increase in severity
vocab.example: The problem of memory loss is compounded by our tendency to reinterpret events.

vocab.definition: to change the original form or meaning in an unnatural way
vocab.example: Each time a message is retold, there is a risk it will be distorted.

vocab.definition: a quotation from a source; the act of referring to a source
vocab.example: In academic writing, proper citation is essential when reporting others' ideas.

vocab.definition: to leave out; to not include
vocab.example: Omitting crucial context when reporting speech is a form of misrepresentation.

vocab.definition: a part or share of the whole; a ratio
vocab.example: Each relay increases the proportion that reflects the reporter's own perspective.

opts: That meaning is preserved perfectly in chains
That communication produces meaning well but preserves it poorly
questions.correct: That communication produces meaning well but preserves it poorly
questions.hint: "Extraordinarily good at producing meaning, and extraordinarily bad at preserving it accurately."

questions.text: What happens to information at each relay in a communication chain?
opts: The total information reduces while the reporter's perspective increases
questions.correct: The total information reduces while the reporter's perspective increases
questions.hint: "Each relay tends to reduce total information transmitted while increasing the proportion that reflects the relayer's own perspective."

questions.correct: Memory reconstructs rather than replays — reflecting what seemed important to him

That journalism is sometimes as powerful as policy (Kamila) vs always more powerful (Daniyar)

questions.correct: Builds back up from parts; creates rather than copies

questions.text: "She argued that journalism SHAPES opinion." — Present Simple used because:
opts: She said it in the past
It's still presented as her current view/general claim
questions.hint: Both are acceptable: "shaped" (backshift applied) or "shapes" (general truth/current view — no shift needed). ✅

questions.text: "He denied taking the money." — "denied" + gerund because:
opts: deny needs a gerund, not an infinitive
questions.correct: deny needs a gerund, not an infinitive
questions.hint: "deny" + GERUND (taking). NEVER "denied to take." ✅ "He denied TAKING the money." ✅
